extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature: scientists and academics (mathematicians, botanists, agriculturists)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and implicit criteria used in reviewing scientific books, collected correspondence, and specialised journals (examples here: a major mathematics monograph, a correspondence volume, and botanical serials). Useful for peer reviewers and editors assessing scholarly works for clarity, usefulness, and editorial quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / Authorial mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: The book should be more than a mere compilation; the author should 'make the subject his own' and write with the air of mastery that only original work can give.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer praises works that are not merely compilations: 'The book is far from being a compilation, for Dr. Hobson has made the subject his own, and writes with the air of mastery that only original work can give.' Originality and genuine authorial command of the topic are high-value attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage / Filling a gap in the literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a systematic account where none existed in the language or field — cover ground not previously mastered in available literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valuable book offers a systematic account in English when none existed before: 'the subject is one of which there was no systematic account in English, and which no previous English writer had ever really mastered.' This criterion values comprehensive, well-selected scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level of generality (theoretical vs practical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose between the 'theoretically general' (most abstract, Dini-like) and the 'practically general' (cases that occur naturally in analysis and applications, Borel's ideal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/reviewers should ask whether theorems are stated in the most abstract possible form or in the special forms that commonly occur in analysis: 'In what special forms do these problems naturally occur in analysis? What are the really important cases?' A balance favoring usable 'practically general' statements can increase usefulness to applied workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness to ordinary workers / inclusion of important cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the presentation helps ordinary practitioners in analysis and applied mathematics to resolve their concrete problems by including the important special cases and forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If too much abstraction is pursued, 'the ordinary worker... is likely to find himself faced by many theoretical difficulties to which he will not easily find an answer.' Therefore include special cases and forms that naturally arise in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter length and logical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters should be of reasonable length and arranged so that related topics are not awkwardly separated; long chapters can hinder readability and logical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long chapters 'do not make a difficult book easier to read, nor do they make it easier for the author to arrive at the proper logical arrangement of the subject-matter' — chapters v and vi are given as examples that should have been broken into shorter parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundance of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Include many illustrative examples to aid understanding, particularly for difficult or abstract material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer explicitly wishes 'to have seen a great many more examples.' Examples help bridge abstract theory and practical application and improve accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter summaries and signposting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide summaries of chapters and clear signposting to help readers navigate dense material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer suggests 'Summaries of the chapters, too, would have been useful;' such summaries aid readers in grasping the structure and main points of long or technical chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of expression and precise terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise, unambiguous language and avoid awkward or misleading phrases; clarity in wording matters in technical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer criticises phrasing such as 'indefinitely great' where simpler, clearer wording ('there is no lower limit') would be preferable. Precise expression prevents confusion even when the author's intent is clear to himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of typography and reader-oriented presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ typographical variety and other 'arts of popularity' where helpful to improve readability; do not be overly sober to the point of reducing accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes the author is 'too sober in his use of different kinds of type' and 'shows too great a contempt for the arts of popularity.' Appropriate typographical choices and readable presentation help reach a wider audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing and production quality
rubrics_metrics.description: High production quality — beautiful and faultless printing — is part of a good scholarly book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book is praised as 'beautifully and almost faultlessly printed,' indicating that physical quality (typography, printing) is an explicit evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour in treatment of difficult technical topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficult or classical areas (e.g., double limits, improper integrals, Fourier series, rigorous treatments of Riemann's work) should be treated with appropriate rigour and final touches of precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer highlights chapter vii (Fourier's Series) as providing 'a final touch of rigour' and praises the treatment of repeated limits. Where necessary the book should supply rigorous arguments even on the hardest parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical placement of foundational topics (sequence of topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce foundational notions (e.g., series) at stages that make subsequent theorems and proofs more coherent and less fragmented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer objects that 'it would have been better to introduce the notion of a series at an earlier stage' because some theorems concerning integrals become separated in an irritating way; proper sequencing improves comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices and critical remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Include appendices for supplementary critical remarks or responses to existing literature, when space permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short appendix containing further critical remarks is noted; such material can be useful for addressing ongoing scholarly debates (e.g., summaries of König's theories and replies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial arrangement and explanatory annotation for correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing letters/correspondence, arrange them for publication with explanatory notes and annotations to give context and historical insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correspondence of Liebig and Gussefeld is commended as 'arranged for publication, with explanatory notes and annotations' — editorial apparatus enhances the value of collected letters to historians and specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and interest to target readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Select material that will be of clear interest to the intended specialists (e.g., scientific agriculturists, historians of chemistry, botanists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Liebig correspondence is said to have 'a twofold interest' — both to scientific agriculturists (practical advice, business hints, analytical information) and historians. Evaluative criterion: relevance to intended audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal/serial value for specialists (botanical works)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good botanical serial should serve as a repository for systematic botany and plant geography, ensure rapid publication of papers with new identifications, include monographs, maps, and ecological or phytogeographical studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes features that make Botanisches Jahrbuch and Das Pflanzenreich valuable: irregular appearance to ensure rapid publication of new identifications; inclusion of monographs, maps, systematic accounts, ecological studies, and summaries representing recent work on orders and genera.
